title: Git Rebase vs Merge: Which One Should You Use?
description: The actual difference between git merge and git rebase, what each does to your history, and a simple rule for picking one.
bodyHtml:
Both commands do the same job — bring changes from one branch into another — but they produce very different history.

Merge

git checkout main
git merge feature

Creates a new merge commit that ties the two branch histories together. Nothing on either branch is rewritten. You get an accurate, if sometimes messy, record of exactly when and how branches diverged and came back together.

Rebase

git checkout feature
git rebase main

Replays your feature branch's commits one by one on top of main's latest commit, as if you'd branched off right now. The result is a straight, linear history with no merge commits — but every replayed commit gets a new hash. This matters: if anyone else has pulled the old commits, rebasing rewrites history out from under them.

The rule of thumb

  • Rebase local, not-yet-pushed commits to keep your own history clean before opening a PR.
  • Never rebase a branch other people are actively working from — merge it instead.
  • Merge is the safe default for integrating a finished feature branch into main.

The golden rule

Don't rebase commits that have already been pushed and could be in use by someone else, unless the whole team knows and agrees (e.g. force-pushing a shared feature branch). Rewriting shared history causes duplicate commits and painful merge conflicts for everyone downstream.
